item.title: ‘We Left in the Clothes We Were Wearing’: Yemenis Flee New Fighting
item.description:
At least half of the population is hungry. Millions of children are unvaccinated. A measles outbreak is spreading.

The people of Yemen have survived the indignities of a more than decade-long civil war. This past week, many were again running for their lives.

A new round of fighting has erupted between the Houthis, the Iran-backed militia in the north, and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government, widening the regional conflict that began early this year with the U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran.

More than 46,000 people fled their homes in the past week alone, a U.N. agency estimated on Friday, some with little more than the clothes on their backs.

Al-Megdad Hashem and his family were among them. At first, one night late last week, they stayed home, kept awake by the sound of shelling. Then, the next morning, shells landed near their house, in the fiercely contested province of Taiz, wounding two people, including Mr. Hashem’s nephew.

The only way to get them to a hospital was to load them onto a truck that normally carries construction materials. All told, he said, 34 people piled in, including Mr. Hashem, his wife, their four children and his elderly parents. They had barely enough time to stuff their belongings into one small bag.

“It was difficult to take anything,” he said. “We want the war to stop so that people can return to their homes.”

The civil war had largely settled into a fragile peace in recent years, since a 2022 U.N.-brokered cease-fire effectively partitioned the country between government- and Houthi-held areas. Now, Yemen is again in the throes of full-fledged fighting, aggravating what was already one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

Making matters worse, the U.N. World Food Program is so short of money that it has suspended food aid altogether and reduced its provision of monthly cash assistance to every other month, Carl Skau, the agency’s acting executive director, said in a phone interview on Thursday. He had visited Yemen last week.

Children were not going to school in the camps for displaced people that he visited, he said. Yemenis told him they were selling their belongings to buy food. And at one health clinic, a long line of mothers were waiting to be seen, with malnourished children in their arms. “They were struggling to afford one meal a day,” he said.

Yemen, he said, has been barraged not only by the fighting. The disruption of shipping in the region has also raised food prices in a country that imports most of what it eats. Meanwhile, droughts and floods have damaged Yemen’s farms. “The little they produce inside is turned upside down by the weather,” Mr. Skau said.

Even before the latest surge in violence, an estimated 4.5 million Yemenis were displaced from their homes. Nearly half of the country’s health facilities are not functional. Attacks on aid workers have forced the United Nations to suspend operations in the Houthi-held north.

This week, Houthi forces captured Mokha, a strategic Red Sea port city in Taiz, as well as an island in the waterway, according to two Yemeni officials, giving the militia a foothold in Bab al-Mandab, a major maritime choke point through which oil from Saudi Arabia passes on its way to Asia.

Houthi forces have also attacked Saudi oil facilities, in turn pushing up already rising global oil prices.

The Houthis have frequently accused Saudi Arabia of striking their positions.

On Friday, the broadcaster Al-Masirah, which is controlled by the militia, said that Saudi Arabia had launched two rounds of airstrikes on the port of Mokha. The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment.

The United Nations said on Thursday that at least 14 civilians were killed in the fighting this past week, including two children.

Last Saturday, in the contested Maqbanah district of Taiz Province, Omar Abdulaziz al-Himyari, 25, fled after hearing shelling nearby. At dawn, he and five family members climbed for two hours by foot to a mountain ridge, their route to the closest road. From there they found a car to the nearest city.

“We left in the clothes we were wearing,” he said. “We couldn’t carry anything because of the situation and the difficult terrain.”

They left behind all of their most valuable belongings, including their cows and goats, their beehives and the grain they had planted in their fields.

For now, Mr. al-Himyari is staying with his brother-in-law and looking for work in the city of Taiz, now crowded with the newly displaced. The prices of flour and rice have shot up at the market. Water must be procured from a tanker, and that too is pricey.

“I honestly don’t know how we will manage our daily needs,” he said.

More than 18 million Yemenis face what the United Nations calls acute food insecurity, with 2.2 million children acutely malnourished.

Disease and medical care also remain pressing concerns. The World Health Organization reported more than 17,600 measles cases in the first seven months of the year. At the main hospital in the government-held city of Marib, maternity and obstetric services have been suspended to make space for trauma care, the W.H.O. said, and dead bodies exceed “available mortuary capacity.”

The crisis is especially dire in the Houthi-held north. United Nations operations have been suspended there since October, when U.N. and other aid workers were detained and U.N. offices were raided by the militia. Seventy-three U.N. staff members remain in Houthi detention, the U.N. relief chief told the Security Council in August.

And although Yemen was once a focus of world aid groups, many major funders of relief, such as the United States, have significantly cut their aid budgets.

Yemen needs $2.2 billion in humanitarian assistance, according to the U.N. relief agency, which said it had received only 20 percent of that.

item.title: An Irish Castle Keeps a Piece of a Times Reporter’s Past
item.description:
Times Insider explains who we are and what we do and delivers behind-the-scenes insights into how our journalism comes together.

Europe is cluttered with castles. Castles here, castles there, so many castles that they can become a monotonous blur of stones to even the widest-eyed tourist.

So why did I decide to write a story about yet another Irish castle? After all, my responsibilities at The New York Times do not include keeping abreast of developments in medieval castles; I’m more of a wandering generalist in the United States.

The answer is it’s personal.

Many years ago, in the early spring of 2000, I needed to breathe different air. The previous year had been lost to a life-threatening illness. Emboldened by clean scans, I fled with my wife and 2-year-old daughter to the west of Ireland, with no plans other than to inhale and exhale.

One evening we found ourselves in the County Galway village of Kinvara, a few miles from where my mother had grown up. The setting swelled the heart: Galway Bay at high tide lapping against the pier, brightly painted shops and pubs in communal huddle — and, rising in the near distance to center it all, Dunguaire Castle.

A few months later, The Times generously assigned this cancer-shaken employee to spend a couple of months sending dispatches from Ireland. Rather than open a home office in the more logical location of Dublin, I chose to set up shop in Kinvara, in the metaphorical shadow of Dunguaire.

Over that summer, my family and I established close friendships in the village that endure to this day. We have been back many times, hiking through the limestone lunarscape of the Burren; attending the annual festival of the boats known as “Galway hookers”; listening to the music at Green’s pub, where the likes of John Prine often showed up; and, yes, visiting Dunguaire Castle, where, for a few euros, you could step into the 16th century.

But during a visit to Kinvara in July, I walked up to Dunguaire to find the gate leading to the castle’s entrance chained shut and a sign saying that the local landmark was closed to the public. I then noticed a crowd of people stepping off a sightseeing bus to visit what was essentially a shuttered attraction.

Sure enough, throughout that day and the days that followed, I saw bus after bus pulling into a nearby parking lot, and dozens and dozens of people trekking up to certain disappointment.

What made this especially puzzling was that Dunguaire isn’t just another castle. The residents of Kinvara will tell you with unabashed pride that Dunguaire is Ireland’s most photographed castle, often featured in its tourism marketing.

Well, I thought. There’s a story here somewhere.

From an international perspective, the reasons for the castle’s closure were, at best, mildly interesting. As my story would lay out — in echo of reporting by several Irish media outlets — the closure was rooted in a familiar dispute among various government agencies over responsibility for operating and maintenance costs.

But I thought this local standoff presented the opportunity for a richer story: a chance to cast the castle as the central character in an article touching on the ghosts that inform everyday life in a small community.

First, I read area histories and talked to local experts about the castle, which was built around 1510 as a defensive lookout and residence. Its name translates to “Fort of Guaire,” after a seventh-century king who, legend has it, was so generous that his right arm grew longer than his left.

Next, I tried to nail down exactly how to pronounce Dunguaire. For 25 years, I had been saying dun-GOO-ruh, only to have a local academic gently tell me that he’d never heard it pronounced that way. It was karmic payback for all the times I’ve haughtily corrected visitors to New York for saying HEW-ston Street, instead of HOW-ston.

To settle the matter, Fran O’Reilly, a retired researcher leading the campaign to reopen Dunguaire, put the question to a few patrons at Fahy’s, a wonderful pub just outside the village. The consensus: doon-GWEER-ah.

Finally, after gathering comments from the various vested parties, I sat down to personify the castle. I imagined the stone structure bearing centuries-long witness to the evolution of a small village on the west coast of Ireland. Through famine and war, prosperity and deprivation, as actors came and went across the Kinvara stage, including more than a few I had come to know.

The publicans and farmers, the shopkeepers and churchgoers. The fisherman forever chasing mackerel and the woman forever baking scones, the businessman glued to his phone and the lost soul surviving on ice cream. The boatman who, at the slightest nod, will sing for you “The Queen of Connemara.”

The castle has seen it all, including an American journalist who paused in Kinvara long ago to breathe in the sea-scented air.

item.title: How One Man’s Quest for a Musketeer’s Bones Got Him Locked Up
item.description:
Wim Dijkman was in Munich the first time I talked to him, in possibly illicit possession of three possibly ancient bones.

The remains — two teeth, one humerus — may or may not belong to what is left of D’Artagnan, the French historical figure upon whom Alexandre Dumas based the main character in “The Three Musketeers.”

They are part of a skeleton Mr. Dijkman and his friends unearthed in an old church near Maastricht, in the Netherlands, earlier this year. To the city’s dismay, they did so without permits, and largely in secret: Even church parishioners weren’t fully informed about the giant dig happening directly in front of their altar.

By the time I reached Mr. Dijkman, in May, local officials had become aware of the excavation and had taken over. They had also, and with evident alarm, insisted upon the return of the bones that Mr. Dijkman had sent to Munich for carbon dating and DNA testing.

“The local authority was not amused that we were digging in the church,” Mr. Dijkman, sitting in a German hotel room, admitted to me over the phone.

If he felt any remorse, it was not obvious. Mr. Dijkman, a retired municipal archaeologist and museum curator, went on to tell me that his former colleagues are “bureaucratic civil servants” who had themselves “never discovered anything of any importance” and who now felt a “need to intervene.”

They were after his glory, if you asked Mr. Dijkman.

“Success has many owners, as they say in Dutch,” he said.

Yet the investigation into whether the bones belong to Charles de Batz de Castelmore d’Artagnan, who died during the Siege of Maastricht in 1673, was about to take twists and turns that might have impressed Dumas himself.

Within days of our conversation, Mr. Dijkman would find himself in a cell at the local police station. Within weeks, he’d be arguing in the local media that he was being framed for grave mistakes in unearthing and processing the skeleton.

Within months, it would become clear that Mr. Dijkman and his band of mostly amateur archaeologists might well have uncovered D’Artagnan’s remains — but the town of Maastricht would allege that they may also have impaired the chances that the world will ever know whether the bones truly belong to the musketeer.

The quest for D’Artagnan’s skeleton would prove to be a story full of power struggles, hubris and hot heads. It continues to consume the little corner of the Netherlands, nestled between Belgium and Germany, where it has unfurled.

D’Artagnan, a mentor and confidant to Louis XIV and the captain-lieutenant of his Musketeers of the Guard, was most famously fictionalized in “The Three Musketeers” in 1844. Dumas painted him as an impulsive but daring young man who befriends Athos, Porthos and Aramis — the titular three musketeers — before rising in rank and prominence. His central role in Dumas’s popular story cemented him as a French national legend.

In this part of the Netherlands, where the real D’Artagnan died, his lore is omnipresent — statues and monuments honor him, a local beer is named for him, locals still point out the spot where he is said to have expired. A pop-up cocktail joint is called b’Artagnan.

In Maastricht, finding D’Artagnan would surely make someone a hero.

Mr. Dijkman, 70, told me — many times — that he is a scientist and not, unlike many of his local associates, a D’Artagnan obsessive. He spent most of his career working as a museum curator and archaeologist for the town of Maastricht, a place with sufficient history to employ its own team. Though he said he had been involved in excavations for human remains, they were not the primary focus of his work.

Still, he has spent the past three decades at least a little bit obsessed with the idea of finding D’Artagnan’s.

The notion first came to him around 2000, when he met Odile Bordaz, a French scholar who is one of the world’s foremost experts on the historical figure. She pointed out that the most enduring mystery about the French hero — one that she, his most detailed biographer, had never been able to solve — was where he was buried. Her own research pointed to a Catholic church in the village of Wolder, just outside of Maastricht’s city center.

“‘You have to find him,’” Mr. Dijkman says Ms. Bordaz told him.

Ms. Bordaz recalled the conversation. “He said to me, ‘I’m an archaeologist, after all — perhaps one day I’ll conduct excavations to discover where D’Artagnan is buried,’” she said.

Mr. Dijkman was busy with other projects: carbon-dating horses buried in a mass grave, exhibiting pieces of local pottery in a Japanese museum. But D’Artagnan remained on his mind. After he retired in 2022, he attended a D’Artagnan conference and got the feeling that the attendees almost expected him to find the bones, given that he was an archaeologist living in Maastricht. He felt pressure to deliver.

“To me, it was important as a fin de carrier, as they say in French,” Mr. Dijkman told me while we stood in a history museum in Maastricht, where he has lived since he was 6 years old. “An end of career.”

Retiring also gave him room to maneuver. As part of the town, he had to have extensive approvals for projects. Now, he was a free agent with a shovel and a mission.

Mr. Dijkman approached leaders of the church in Wolder, who were intrigued enough that they set up a foundation in late 2024 to fund the enterprise.

Jos Valke, a deacon, was particularly excited.

“I thought, when we have a treasure in the ground — if God gave us a treasure — then we should use it,” Mr. Valke said.

If they found D’Artagnan, he thought, they could set up a museum in the church. Years of declining attendance and pricey upkeep bills had been straining the 12 Catholic parishes of Maastricht. Capitalizing on the legend of D’Artagnan might offer the financial wherewithal to help fund the whole network.

At first, the quest was both above ground and aboveboard. Mr. Dijkman and Mr. Valke began by using metal detectors to search the church, which had been reconstructed in the late 1800s over the foundations of the medieval structure.

The men were delighted when they detected something near the front of the sanctuary, close to what they believed must have been the altar of the old church. Who but the most revered of figures would have been buried at the altar?

The church exploration fund had only about 4,000 euros in it, though. Hiring a team of qualified archaeologists and anthropologists to dig in the hot spot would have cost about 11,400 euros, Mr. Dijkman estimated. They simply could not afford it. Nor had they consulted local authorities on whether they could dig in the structure.

That might have been a good moment to stop.

But “I said, Yeah, I’m on the threshold of finding him,” Mr. Dijkman said.

The decision was made to press ahead, but quietly. In interviews, Mr. Dijkman alternated between insisting that they thought that going forward was legal because the site was on church property and done with the approval of the church board — and acknowledging that the team knew that it was tap-dancing on the edge of the official rulebook.

“Jos Valke was aware that it was not completely legal, of course,” he told me, of the deacon. During our interviews, Mr. Valke said he thought it was legal.

Mr. Dijkman had other friends along to help with the dig, including Thomas Samek, a physician whose medical expertise seemed potentially beneficial. Mr. Samek was a good fit for another reason: He is a D’Artagnan impersonator, for which he dresses in full regalia and rides a shining steed.

Mr. Valke said that while the church board approved the search, they kept it covert because they “didn’t want a fuss.” Mr. Dijkman didn’t want to publicize the dig before they knew if they had succeeded.

Stories vary regarding how Mr. Dijkman’s crew kept the excavation a secret from church parishioners, but it clearly involved covering up the chasm so that churchgoers could traverse the site to take Holy Communion. And eventually, Mr. Valke built a wooden platform to cover the hole, pulling a faded faux-oriental rug over it before Mass on Sundays.

The dig started slowly. The first set of stones yielded little, Mr. Valke said. But after they had pulled 75 heavy tiles out of the floor — working on Saturdays, per Mr. Dijkman; at night, per Mr. Valke — they finally found what they had been looking for.

There were bones in the earth.

The diggers cleared the dirt from the pit, placing it in white bags and storing it in an ornate church closet. (Mr. Valke is hoping to one day bottle it, and to sell the earth that once held D’Artagnan as a way to raise proceeds for the church.)

Before long, they had uncovered a full skeleton. They shot videos of Mr. Dijkman crouching in the crevasse, pulling sandy dirt away from aged vertebrae as someone else pointed an air compressor at the remains.

Mr. Dijkman started to box up the bones in plastic packaging and transport them to his home, at times placing their plastic containers in the blue Albert Heijn plastic grocery bags that are ubiquitous in this part of Europe.

Why not just leave he bones in situ, one might wonder? The diggers were nervous that if they left the bones in the church, the artifacts might be thrown away by cleaning staff. One wouldn’t want the janitor to toss out the mandible of one of France’s greatest war heroes.

Everything was going well until mid-February — Mr. Dijkman can pinpoint the date, because it was Carnival.

By Mr. Valke’s account, it was around that time that the church started to hear from universities. He alleges that Mr. Dijkman had told them about the dig.

“We thought: We want to be in charge,” Mr. Valke said, explaining that the church decided to go to the town with the find.

Mr. Dijkman emphatically denies this. His contention? Mr. Valke saw a town archaeologist at a local watering hole, Au Mouton Blanc.

“Jos Valke told him, ‘We have found him!’” Mr. Dijkman said.

This still burns for two reasons: It blew their cover and, in Mr. Dijkman’s view, it misplaced the credit for the discovery. “When you say, ‘We have found him,’ you don’t say, ‘Wim has found him,’” Mr. Dijkman explained.

Mr. Valke acknowledged that he “casually” mentioned the discovery to the archaeologist at the bar. But he said that the archaeologist didn’t really react and that “it was just drunken rambling rather than a serious conversation.”

Regardless, after hearing from the church board, the local authorities swooped in to take over. On March 13, they completed the dig.

Officials were alarmed by the state of the grave. Bone fragments in the soil were no longer in their original place — they were mixed together. Part of the skeleton was already unearthed. Pieces were missing.

When local media interviewed Mr. Valke, he implied that stones in the church floor had been loose and that repair work had triggered the find.

Mr. Samek, the D’Artagnan impersonator who had been present for the dig, was alarmed by this: “Jos Valke invented the story,” he said in an email. “That shocked me, because the truth is sacred to me.” (Mr. Valke and Mr. Dijkman both said that it was originally one of the town archaeologists who came up with the construction story.)

It did not take long for finger pointing to begin. The municipality swiftly reported the team of initial diggers, and their lack of appropriate permits, to official cultural heritage authorities.

The church board and Mr. Valke began to suggest in media interviews that Mr. Dijkman had led them to believe that their actions were legal.

By early summer, the town had announced that the initial dig “was not documented according to standard archaeological procedures.”

“As a result, a significant amount of archaeological information has been irreversibly lost,” a town F.A.Q. on the situation read.

Even after they came under scrutiny, Mr. Valke and Mr. Dijkman remained hopeful that they might soon have answers about whether the skeleton was D’Artagnan’s. Mr. Samek had taken several bones to a university in Munich for tests and DNA analysis.

The results, they hoped, could be compared with DNA from the living relatives of the D’Artagnan family.

But then Maastricht announced that it would view those results as null and void: “Because the origin, sampling and documentation of that material were not carried out or verified as part of the current research, it cannot serve as a reliable basis for answering the research question,” the town said in a question-and-answer sheet.

The indignant municipal authorities asked that the original diggers and the university doing the analysis swiftly return the bones. Mr. Dijkman became concerned that the town was going to have what might be D’Artagnan’s bones mailed back from Munich. To protect the precious artifacts from the post, he decided to pick them up himself.

When he arrived back in Maastricht, he refused to turn over the bones — in part, he said, because the town wouldn’t reimburse his travel costs. He entrusted the fragments to a “friend,” hoping that the town would pay him back.

Plus, he wanted to retain a foothold on his project. “I thought: If you give them everything, they can keep you out of everything,” Mr. Dijkman said.

Instead of a reimbursement check, Mr. Dijkman received a visit from several police officers, which came as a shock because he had never had trouble with the law.

He was taken to the station and placed in a cell, he estimates for about four hours. Only after he agreed to cough up the bones — police officers took him in their car to the house of his “friend” to retrieve them — was he released. He has not been formally charged.

Mr. Valke, too, was called into a police station for two and a half hours of questioning. Until he got the summons, he said, it had never occurred to him that he might be under scrutiny for wrongdoing.

By early summer, the town of Maastricht was emphasizing that the bones might not belong to D’Artagnan. While the skeleton is a male of roughly the right age (D’Artagnan is thought to have been about 62 when he died), carbon dating suggests the person was buried sometime between 1500 and 1900. A lot of 62-year-olds died during that span.

An analysis by Saxion University of Applied Sciences in Deventer suggested that the skeleton belonged to a man who ate a diet heavy in fish earlier in life. The town says that appears inconsistent with D’Artagnan’s upbringing, given that he was born far from a coast.

The DNA analysis in Munich was never made public, and a new DNA analysis is being conducted on the skeleton. It is expected to be completed by the end of 2026 or early 2027.

The town has also blasted the initial dig for making identification harder. Several of the bones jumbled together from the earlier excavation have been determined to belong to other people, according to the municipality.

“This is a former colleague who was the first to carry out excavations,” Gilbert Soeters, one of the town archaeologists, told reporters at a news conference in July, according to Agence France-Presse. “Well, the term excavations is not quite appropriate. These were not archaeological excavations.”

Mr. Dijkman says that the town is suggesting he messed up the dig so that it can take credit if the remains turn out to be D’Artagnan’s. Mr. Valke, meanwhile, is stressed about possible legal repercussions. Mr. Samek called the entire messy situation a “pity.”

“It’s a shame, because Pierre-Alexandre Dumas’s motto was the Musketeer one: ‘All for one, and one for all,’” agreed Ms. Bordaz, the French scholar. “So, you know, we would have liked things to be in that spirit.”

Still, they all share a hope that the man in the grave will indeed prove to be d’Artagnan.

“At that time, there will be a reaction from the French authorities,” Mr. Dijkman tells me. “They will say: How will you continue to frame the man who found our national hero?”

Koba Ryckewaert contributed reporting.

item.title: In Flood-Stricken Nepal, a Cool Gust Carries Hopes of a Miracle Rescue
item.description:
Deep beneath the Himalayas, six men were harnessing the fierce force of glacial melt that provides electricity to Nepal when a terrible deluge struck, filling their workplace, an underground powerhouse, with a churn of silt, rock and water. Floor by floor, life was extinguished.

But two and a half weeks after that devastating flooding, rescue crews digging through a silt-swamped tunnel at the Chilime hydropower project have made a tantalizing discovery. The area toward the top of the five-floor underground facility appears to be fed by a pocket of air.

In a drowned and battered landscape, the presence of oxygen, cool and fresh according to rescue workers, lit faint hopes that the six workers — the only ones still unaccounted for at the facility — might have somehow survived.

Chances of life are still slim. While three workers were pulled out of tunnels at other hydropower projects on the ninth and 10th days after the floods, another week has now passed. The floods have killed at least 1,385 people in Nepal and left 5,130 missing, along with hundreds more unaccounted for in neighboring Tibet.

Still, for days, rescue crews brought in by helicopter — Nepali and Indian soldiers, veteran mountaineers, Australian engineers and locals who had themselves lost relatives to the natural disaster — clawed through the silt by hand, sometimes crouching on planks to prevent the earth from claiming them, too. Efforts to pump out the sludge failed. Roads and bridges in the mountainous region were washed away, so heavy machinery could not be brought in to excavate the tunnel until Friday, 17 days after the floods.

“My heart is breaking for the six workers, and we have to do everything to try to save them, if there is even a small, small chance,” said Kulman Ghising, the former managing director of the Chilime Hydropower Company, who has lent his expertise to the recovery effort.

More than 900 hydropower workers are dead or missing from the floods, which appear to have been caused by a plummeting chunk of glacier and bedrock. Fourteen hydropower projects were destroyed, along with a large solar power station. Roughly 10 percent of Nepal’s electricity generation was wiped out, in a country that counts hydropower as one of its major exports.

Mr. Ghising, who, as the longtime head of the Nepal Electricity Authority, presided over the rapid electrification of one of Asia’s poorest nations, said he had personally hired one of the six men who is believed to be trapped in the powerhouse. He also helped build six hydropower projects in the region.

“In one, two moments, everything is gone, everything we built for decades,” he said.

The rush of water, debris and mud from the Trishuli River in Nepal swept into the 820-foot tunnel to Chilime’s underground powerhouse, choking it shut. As of Saturday night, the crews had fully cleared about 200 feet of the tunnel, with a route in the upper part excavated deeper. For days, they had used buckets, shovels and bare hands, “digging like a rabbit,” according to Manish Bista, the plant manager.

Then, on Friday night, heavy machinery brought via a newly cleared road finally started to move earth in the tunnel. But hours later, a wheel loader tumbled over. Another machine suffered a flat tire. Most supplies are still flown in by helicopters landing on a perilous patch of riverside.

“We are isolated on all sides,” said Baburaja Maharjan, the current managing director of Chilime Hydropower, who has been at the rescue site since the day the flood struck. “We have no spare parts or machines. We have very limited resources.”

The teams are now working 24 hours a day, with no way out if another big flood were to come, Mr. Maharjan said.

But late this week, a breakthrough spurred on the exhausted rescue crews.

As Nepali Army soldiers crawled into a crevice in the muck, about 350 feet into the tunnel, they felt a gust of cool air through a tiny gap. Yelling into the space, they heard an echo and determined that there was an air pocket ahead.

One tunnel in the underground network slopes upward and connects to the top floor of the powerhouse. Rescue crews think that this tunnel may be free of debris as it inclines. Mr. Maharjan said that during emergencies, the engineers stationed in the powerhouse have been trained to run from their computer stations one story below to an assembly point on the top floor. That area may also have access to filtered water and a basic kitchen, where workers usually cooked their instant noodles or rice and lentils.

“There is some hope of life inside,” Mr. Maharjan said. “That is why we are continuing with extremely difficult work.”

Saroj Pandey is one of the six workers who was on duty in the powerhouse when the deluge came, according to Chilime directors and engineers.

Mr. Pandey, a computer engineer, was married two years ago and welcomed his first child last year, according to friends. One of them, Swoorup Joshi, lives in Australia and used to spend hours video chatting with Mr. Pandey, playing guitar or just talking about life.

Hours before the flood, Mr. Joshi texted his friend a single word: “Bro.”

Mr. Pandey did not respond.

“He’s just a chill, happy guy,” said Mr. Joshi, who created a website to document the efforts to locate the missing men. “I can’t imagine he’s gone.”

item.title: In the Home of Volvo and Spotify, an Election Shows Shifting Priorities
item.description:
Gun violence in Sweden has dropped after surging for years.

Top Swedish companies, like Volvo, IKEA and Spotify, remain global powerhouses, helping the economy grow faster than most places in Europe.

And Sweden has produced more billionaires than just about any country its size.

With national elections set for Sunday and the big picture reasonably good, one might think that Sweden’s incumbent center-right government would cruise back to power.

But the issues that matter most to voters have shifted in ways that have helped left-leaning political parties, bucking a trend in Europe. The latest polls show a center-left coalition with a narrow lead over its center-right rivals before voting starts.

Scandinavia is often ahead of the curve when it comes to social trends, and Sweden (as well as Denmark) offers a picture of what might happen when hot-button issues like migration recede and voters swing their attention elsewhere.

That does not mean that Sweden’s far-right politicians, who have propped up the current government, are a spent force. In fact, if the right manages to squeak to victory, it has promised, for the first time, to give them a share of power.

That would be a seismic change in Sweden and another victory for Europe’s nationalists, following the far right’s success in Germany’s recent elections.

A decade ago, Sweden welcomed huge numbers of migrants, which prompted a backlash, just as it did in many places. Then the pandemic hit. Then Russia invaded Ukraine, causing energy prices to spike and leaving Swedes, like many Europeans, feeling less secure.

Right-wing parties in Sweden, like those in Britain, Italy, France and Germany, tapped into that unease and grew more popular.

Today, compared to other parts of Europe, Sweden’s economy has bounced back faster, and inflation, migration and shootings have decreased. As a result, analysts say, the political winds have turned.

“It was a tougher situation four years ago,” said Jens Rydgren, a sociology professor at Stockholm University.

As he munched on a chokladboll (a freshly rolled chocolate ball) at a Stockholm bakery, Mr. Rydgren said that many Swedes were refocusing on the classic Scandinavian priorities: public health care, good schools, the environment.

“And traditionally, the center left owns these issues,” he said.

The party leading the polls is the Social Democrats, the country’s stalwart center-left organization, at 27 percent. With its allies, the left is predicted to get 51 percent of the vote.

Sweden’s No. 2 most popular party is the Sweden Democrats. The organization has neo-Nazi roots and is polling at 19 percent, a remarkably high level for what was once a fringe party. Its popularity has stayed relatively steady even if its more centrist allies have lost some steam.

At a Sweden Democrat rally the other night, Jimmie Akesson, the party leader, paced a stage lit up with pyrotechnics.

“Do you remember what Sweden looked like four years ago?” he belted out. “Do we want to go back to that?”

“No!” the crowd yelled back.

The Sweden Democrats hold the most seats in Parliament on their side of the aisle and their support shores up the center-right coalition. The government has adopted many of their tough-on-crime policies and imposed a much harsher immigration system, tightening up the rules on asylum seekers and making it easier to deport people.

But because of the Sweden Democrats’ past connections to white supremacist groups, the party was not given any ministries.

This election could change that. The Sweden Democrats have asked for half the seats in the cabinet if a center-right coalition returns to power. If that happens, it would radically alter the direction of the country, with the government taking an even more severe approach to migration and crime.

Christopher Jarnvall, a Sweden Democrat municipal official in the town of Norrköping, said that if Sweden didn’t insist that immigrants embrace a traditional Swedish identity, the country’s cohesion would be at stake.

“We want to make Sweden Sweden again,” he said, echoing a far-right slogan.

In Sweden’s previous general election, 84 percent of eligible voters cast ballots. The country, with its 11 million people, tends to get excited about elections.

“Valstugor,” or election cabins, pop up across the country, in town squares or busy areas, where party workers mingle with voters.

On Thursday, in downtown Stockholm, Mohammed Al-isawi, 19, bobbed through the crowd. Born in Iraq and now a student with a part-time job, he fled the war and came to Sweden 10 years ago with his family. He’s voting for the first time and leaning left.

He said he was troubled by the anti-immigrant talk coming from the right.

“That feels rather extreme,” he said.

The polls close at 8 p.m. local time, and preliminary results are expected three hours later.

But Sweden’s political landscape is fragmented among more than a half-dozen parties, including the Moderates, the Liberals, the Green Party and the Christian Democrats. Analysts say that negotiations to form the next government could take days or even weeks.

item.title: Trump’s Tariffs Tear at the Bond Between Twin Border Towns
item.description:
Before Matthew Shoemaker became mayor of Sault Ste. Marie — before he could read or ride a bike, even — he knew what formed the bedrock of his hometown: the Algoma Steel factory, and the Michigan town across the river.

Sitting at his desk this month, both weighed heavily on him.

For over a century, Sault Ste. Marie has grown around Algoma Steel. Now, the Trump administration’s tariffs on Canadian steel exports threaten to devastate the local economy and its 80,000 people. And the close bond with the city’s border twin in Michigan has been ruptured as a consequence of the escalating trade war between the two nations. Canadians, who frequently cross the border to live parts of their lives on the other side of the river, are hurt, angry and no longer feel welcome in the United States.

“The tariffs are so specific to our main industry that it feels personal, it feels like the American administration is attacking Sault Ste. Marie,” Mr. Shoemaker, 37, said in an interview this month.

Mr. Shoemaker’s own father worked at Algoma Steel. His mother immigrated from Italy after World War II, sponsored by an uncle who worked at the mill. So did the brothers who came with her, and her sisters’ husbands.

“It is a central entity in the history of so many people’s families here,” Mr. Shoemaker said. “The fact that it has fallen on hard times causes a real emotional reaction.”

More than half of the steel produced in Sault Ste. Marie used to be shipped to the United States, and the 50 percent tariffs imposed by the Trump administration have devastated the company’s finances.

In March, Algoma Steel, one of only three major Canada-based steel producers, abruptly laid off 1,000 workers it had planned to phase out over two or more years through retirements and reassignments.

Mr. Shoemaker believes the real toll could reach 3,000 jobs, once the layoffs’ full impact makes its way through the city’s broader economy. And things are not getting better soon.

Talks between the United States and Canada broke down last month, and hoped-for tariff relief for steel did not materialize.

The Canadian government has supported Algoma Steel through previous downturns — it has gone bust four times in its history — and will direct a steel contract for the construction of icebreakers to the company. But that will not make up for the loss of the U.S. contracts that form the core of its client base.

“The Soos” — as Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, and Sault Ste. Marie, Mich., are affectionately known — were born as one village on opposite banks of a river, settled by French Jesuit missionaries in 1668. They were later divided as the St. Marys River became the international border between the United States and Canada.

But the twin towns stayed knit together.

An American, Francis Clergue, founded a steel and iron company on the Canadian side in 1901, drawn by a nearby mine and a waterway that could carry the processed metals to the U.S. market.

The Soos grew in tandem — the Canadian one significantly bigger — and for the next 125 years, aside from during the pandemic, the border was an afterthought.

Canadians crossed to Michigan regularly for cheaper gas, good bars and holidays at nearby campsites. Americans brought their children to the Canadian side for sports practice at the local pool and hockey rink, and the two towns maintained a slew of shared social activities, mostly on the Canadian side, which has more infrastructure.

But traffic over the bridge from Ontario into Michigan fell by a quarter last year after President Trump’s first round of tariffs, as people in Sault Ste. Marie, like many Canadians, expressed their anger by canceling visits.

Carlo Lucio, 62, said he had no qualms paying a few extra dollars to fill up his car on the Ontario side instead of Michigan, which had been his weekly routine before the tariffs. He retired from Algoma in 2024 after 36 years and counted himself lucky to have left with a full pension just before the tariffs hit.

Harder was pulling out of pool tournaments in the United States, the hobby he most looked forward to. After much thought, he skipped one, though in recent months he had been toying with the idea of returning.

“When the trade talks broke down, I said I can’t even think about going back,” Mr. Lucio said. “The U.S. government has made it very clear. They are not welcoming Canadians.”

His biggest worry now is for his former colleagues. One of them is Mike Caruso, 49, who worked alongside Mr. Lucio and was among the 1,000 people laid off in March.

Mr. Caruso rushed to find a new job, one that takes him to a mine in northern Ontario two weeks a month. “I’m lucky,” he said, despite the strain it puts on family life. “There’s 1,000 guys out there looking for work.”

The deep bonds between the two Soos were built by more than steel. For some people, crossing the border has meant belonging.

Ginny Cymbalist moved to the Michigan Soo in 1970, and one of the first things she did, she said, was cross the bridge to the nearest synagogue — in Ontario. Jews from both sides of the border have congregated in the Ontario Soo as far back as 125 years ago. Congregation Beth Jacob was built in 1945, anchoring the small cross-border community that today counts about 35 families.

“I got married there,” Ms. Cymbalist, 82, said in a phone interview from her home in Michigan. “My sons had their bar mitzvahs there.” She and her late husband both served as presidents of the congregation over the decades.

She is still in Ontario several times a week, including this past week for Rosh Hashana. Ms. Cymbalist said that the trade war was deeply upsetting.

“I’m quite concerned. There is a lot of frustration about the tariffs; I hear the anger, they’re hurt,” she said of her Canadian friends.

Despite the close ties within the Jewish community, Tova Arbus, the congregation president, worries that the trade war could still cause a strain. Just this summer, one Ontario couple said they were not comfortable crossing into Michigan for an annual Jewish retreat held there.

“They were very firmly, like, we’re not going into the States,” Ms. Arbus said.

On a warm evening this month, roughly 6,000 people from the Soos poured into the local hockey arena on the Canadian side for a concert by the rock star Bryan Adams.

Mr. Adams, who is himself from an Ontario border town, has been outspoken about the trade war and released a new single this summer, “51st State,” denouncing Mr. Trump’s repeated assertion that Canada should be part of the United States.

Mr. Adams said it was important for artists to speak up, adding that one friend he had asked to collaborate on his coming album, which is mostly about Canada, told him he was worried about losing his U.S. green card. “People are scared,” he said in an interview just before going onstage.

But the threats from the Trump administration, he added, are pulling Canada together. “This kind of rhetoric that’s coming from south of the border is uniting a lot of Canadians, in a way I’ve never seen in my lifetime,” Mr. Adams said.

About two hours into the show, after his biggest hits had left the crowd sweaty and tired, Mr. Adams said he would play a new song. The audience fell quiet and then erupted in cheers at the chorus — a defiant refusal to accept annexation, set to a driving beat — “You might have too much on your plate, go on load us up with tariffs, but we’ll never be the 51st state.”

item.title: Along Himalayan Floods’ Path, Wiped Out Towns and Mounting Grief
item.description:
Taking a break from the noisy work of leading a school of over 500 students, Madhav Lamichhane would ride his motorbike down to the riverside Betrawati Bazaar every week. The principal skipped the busy shops around the town’s clock tower, preferring a quiet moment by the Ram temple to take in the “very beautiful flow” of the Trishuli River.

But on Aug. 26, as he was in school preparing for the first morning bell, the river below suddenly became a violent torrent that obliterated much of the town of Betrawati, erasing its square from the map. It left no trace of the temple, the market or the concrete bridges, and only fragments of the hundreds of homes that dotted either side of the river.

Mr. Lamichhane and the school, up on a hillside, escaped its wrath.

But about 200 students did not. The younger children, ages 5 to 11, had been waiting in the riverside town for a yellow school bus. The oldest, backpacks strapped on, had been slowly making their way uphill to the school when the deluge swallowed them.

“What can I say to the river?” Mr. Lamichhane sighed. He said that fewer than a third of the town’s families had scraped through without losing anyone, with many wiped out entirely.

“It was very beautiful previously,” he said. “It is a cultural and historical place, too. But all that became the past.”

When part of a Himalayan glacier near Nepal’s border with Tibet collapsed late last month, the ferocious water and debris that barreled through the gorge wiped out almost everything in their path for tens of miles. Two weeks later, the death toll stands at over 1,300, with 5,000 others missing, many most likely buried beneath the mud.

In the days after the floods, reporters from The New York Times traveled along the path of destruction, trying to reach areas cut off in a poor country with difficult terrain. What we found was towns and villages wiped off the map. Small reminders of life before remained in the sludge: a buried roof jutting out from the mud, a student’s backpack, an empty reading glasses case.

CHINA

TIBET

Avalanche site

NEPAL

Reporters’ journey

Kathmandu

Route starting point

The dozens of bridges and the tens of miles of destroyed roads will surely be rebuilt. Technical assessments are already underway for a financing plan. The expected billions in costs will add to the debt of a small country still paying back loans it took to rebuild after a catastrophic earthquake just over a decade ago.

But helping to count the number of dead and telling the stories of wiped out communities is left to loved ones who were away at the time or who climbed to higher ground as the water closed in — now unsure whether to consider themselves lucky to have survived, or cursed to bear the crushing grief and loneliness.

The only lifeline connecting the remains of those settlements is a narrow dirt track that skirts the hills. The drive between some of the towns, which would have taken 15 minutes before the floods, took us seven to eight hours — the path was jammed with traffic and frequently blocked by mudslides caused by the last of the monsoon rains.

The Chilime hydropower tunnel, 10 miles from the border with China, was as far as we could get before the road collapsed into a dirt track along the river that was not safe to trek. Helicopters frequently flew through the narrow gorge on search and rescue operations to several tunnels in the area, where workers are feared trapped.

Officials who had flown into Syrabrubesi and Timure — the stretch beyond what was accessible by road — and survivors who were airlifted out said that hundreds of buildings had vanished, with nearly 1,000 people missing.

“The area is deserted now,” said Dolma Thangjen Sherpa, an elected member of the ward where Syabrubesi is, who was sheltering in a monastery in Kathmandu.

In the urban pockets along our journey — from Kathmandu to an army base and to a city nearly 100 miles downstream from where the floods originated that saw over 350 bodies wash up on its riverbanks — people flipped through lists of the dead, which ran multiple pages, and searched for clues in the lines of mangled bodies.

Most left in disappointment. Kami Delma Sherpa stared at a photograph of a woman with a golden tooth posted on the wall outside a hospital in Kathmandu, thinking she had finally found her sister, who worked at the border crossing. But when she went inside and looked at the body, it was not her.

As we traveled along the floods’ path of destruction, there were still small miracles to celebrate.

CHINA

TIBET

Avalanche site

NEPAL

Area of flooding

Betrawati

Dhunge Bazaar

Reporters’ journey

Kathmandu

A green house in Dhunge Bazaar remained standing, saving its residents, who had watched from their balcony as a whirlpool of mud and debris threatened to close in on them. A principal evacuated all of his students to safety, before his school was washed away. Three of the hundreds of workers trapped in hydropower project tunnels were pulled out alive more than a week after the floods.

Another unlikely escape was hiding in plain sight. We watched night fall over Betrawati last Friday, staring at a three-story house buried so deep in the sludge that only its roof and a sliver of its upper windows were visible. The search and rescue teams had moved on, the disposal of a decaying cow their last act that afternoon.

As we began our drive out of the ghost town late at night, we could hear only crickets and the roar of water. No one knew that a woman, Chandika Shrestha, was still clinging to life inside the house. Her family was among hundreds who had resigned themselves to their loss and had begun final ceremonial rites by cremating effigies of their loved ones.

The next day, locals heard a faint cry. Rescuers scrambled to dig her out.

But those kinds of miracles were few.

Betrawati, the site of a 1792 treaty that ended a war between Nepal’s kingdom and the Qing dynasty, laid bare the extent of the floods’ devastation.

What was once the town square, surrounded by lush paddy fields, now looks desolate — as if it had always been a riverbed, but the stream had shrunk. The two-story police station had been uprooted and deposited hundreds of feet away. A school bus with red seats was flipped on its side. Strewed around it were school bags, baby sandals, a broken speaker. A stench filled the air.

Pavitra Lamichhane, 32, took us to the riverbed to show where the house she had lived in with her 12-year-old son and mother-in-law once stood. She had been “going mad” searching for her son, her only hope, but they all survived.

With her husband, who died in a car accident two years ago, they had built a house in concrete to help it withstand earthquakes. But it was no match for the wall of mud from above.

“See that tree,” said Ms. Lamichhane, pointing to the ridge as her reference. “This should be the spot.”

Officials estimated that of a population of a little over 1,000 people, 315 people were lost in Betrawati. A large number of the survivors are homeless, sheltering on higher ground. In one hostel, aid workers prepared warm meals for 200 people. A generator hummed, powering mobile charging points for about 300 people.

The school where Mr. Lamichhane is principal had become the town’s relief hub, with trucks offloading aid material and social workers trying to console and entertain children uprooted from their homes.

On the morning of the floods, as Mr. Lamichhane was preparing for the day in his office, he got a call from the school bus driver saying he had heard of flooding upstream.

The driver had delivered two busloads of students to the school and was on his way to the town square for his final run.

“I scrolled on my mobile but did not see any news of the flood,” the principal said. He phoned a friend upriver, who told him the market had collapsed. “The flood is coming,” the friend exclaimed.

Mr. Lamichhane told staff to evacuate the 250 students already at the school to the forested areas above, while he and others rushed down toward the river to see what they could do.

He called anyone and everyone he could reach along the river: his staff who had not arrived at school yet, the parents of students.

Two phone calls, in particular, haunt him.

The first was to his elementary schoolteacher, whose riverside house he had often visited for a cup of tea. She had told him, “We are escaping! We are escaping!”

“The connection was lost,” he said. “She is among the missing.”

He remembers the second call, to another colleague, Ajay Kumar Yadav, with anger.

“I told him to come out. But he did not believe that the river could come up to there,” he said. “And he lost his life.”

As the principal spoke, he took his cap off to show his head, which he had shaved in a ritual performed to mourn dead relatives. (He lost two cousins who had been truck drivers along the border.)

Attendance had not yet been taken when the floods came, making identifying the missing students a challenge.

When we asked if he had to rely on families reporting their children as missing, he said, “There is no family to report,” adding, “The families are gone.”

Closer to the border with China, in the hillside village of Thulo Bharkhu, just before the road collapsed, a Buddhist monk held a vigil at his home for three members of his family — his son and two daughters-in-law — who were lost in the flood.

CHINA

TIBET

NEPAL

Area of flooding

Reporters’ journey

Kathmandu

Singi Nurpu Lama is 80 and has difficulty walking. But he still went to other homes in the village to help lead their mourning prayers.

“There was flooding in the past also, but nothing like this,” the monk said.

One of the monk’s sons, Kshokyal Dorje Lama, was working in a bank in Kathmandu when he heard news of the flooding. He worried about his wife, Pratima Tamang, a nurse who was elected four years ago as the local municipality’s vice chairperson.

Mr. Lama tried to reach her on the phone, and the call went through.

“I felt like she was running, but I couldn’t hear anything,” he said. “Then the connection was lost.”

The couple had fallen in love when Ms. Tamang was still in nursing school and later married in a two-day ceremony in the village with over 1,000 guests. The houses were decorated with strings of lights. There was a feast of meat and rice and drinks. A large group of guests sang and performed a circle dance to celebrate.

Ms. Tamang could have gone abroad for better pay, as many Nepali nurses do. But she chose to go back to the village. The couple had planned to have their first child soon.

“I feel so alone,” he said. “Like fish without water.”

Maps by Pablo Robles.

item.title: Okinawa Set to Elect Conservative Amid Fears About China and Economy
item.description:
A 42-year-old conservative politician was projected to prevail on Sunday in the race to be governor of Okinawa, a win for Japan’s hawkish prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, as she seeks to accelerate a military buildup to counter China.

Genta Koja, a deputy mayor of Naha, the Okinawan capital, was expected to unseat a two-term governor, Denny Tamaki, who had criticized Ms. Takaichi’s defense policies and opposed the construction of new American armed forces facilities on Okinawa island. When he takes office later this month, Mr. Koja will be the youngest governor in the history of the Okinawa prefecture, a group of subtropical islands in southern Japan.

NHK, the public broadcaster, relying on exit poll data, said that Mr. Koja had won about 60 percent of the votes on Sunday, compared with about 40 percent for Mr. Tamaki, the son of a Japanese mother and a U.S. Marine, who had the backing of left-leaning parties in Japan.

“I interpret the results as a choice by many to move Okinawa forward,” Mr. Koja said in a comment to NHK on Sunday after he was projected to win.

Only about 2 percent of votes had been tallied as of late Sunday, but they showed Mr. Koja in the lead.

Mr. Tamaki conceded the election in a statement, saying: “I want to heed the will of the people. There was still much I wanted to accomplish in a third term, but I intend to use this result as a source of strength.”

Mr. Koja’s expected victory would be a blow to Okinawa’s pacifist movement, which for years has opposed the American military presence on the island. Okinawa, with a population of 1.5 million, hosts 70 percent of Japan’s American bases despite accounting for only 0.6 percent of the country’s landmass. (The United States seized Okinawa from Japan after World War II; it returned the island in 1972 but has continued to operate bases there.)

Many members of older generations, who still have memories of the war, have rejected the central government’s plans to make Okinawa a bulwark in its efforts to counter Chinese military aggression. They say the presence of more troops makes the island even more of a target.

Ms. Takaichi, who took office last year, has pushed forward with plans to further militarize Okinawa by sending more troops to the area and expanding missile and electronic warfare capabilities.

Okinawa, the southernmost prefecture of Japan, is strategically significant because it sits close to China and Taiwan. It has long had a large American military footprint, with roughly 30,000 active-duty personnel, which has been a source of tension on the island for decades, amid concerns about pollution, noise and crime.

Mr. Koja, who was backed by Ms. Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic Party and other conservative parties, had expressed a willingness during the campaign to work with the Americans. He said he would support a plan to transfer a busy air base used by the Marines from southern Okinawa to a less populated coastal area in the north. Mr. Tamaki had fiercely opposed the plan for years and made it a signature campaign issue.

Mr. Koja also spoke forcefully about rising security threats in the region, including from China, and the need to modernize Japan’s military, known as the Self-Defense Forces.

“It is an undeniable fact that the security environment surrounding Okinawa has become increasingly severe, making the Japan-U.S. security alliance and the deterrent capabilities of the Self-Defense Forces essential,” he said at a debate last month.

There has been rising concern in Okinawa about China’s growing assertiveness in recent years, especially among younger islanders, who were core to Mr. Koja’s victory, according to exit poll data reported by NHK.

Yet despite geopolitical questions, voters appeared most concerned about the economy. Wages in Okinawa are below the national average; prices have risen; and unemployment and child poverty are concerns in many areas.

Mr. Koja promised to put in place policies that would help lift wages, and he said he would provide more support to parents for child care. He also vowed to do more to promote tourism.

Masaaki Gabe, a professor emeritus at the University of the Ryukyus in Okinawa, said Mr. Koja would face pressure to improve the economy.

“The people of Okinawa want prosperity,” he said.

Yet for Okinawan citizens, including the crowds of pacifist activists who still hold regular protests outside American bases, it is becoming increasingly difficult to oppose the defense buildup, Mr. Gabe said, as the central government has grown more assertive in its push to militarize the region.

“The situation has reached a point,” he said, “where the prefecture has almost no authority to resist.”

item.title: Iran Will Meet With Gulf Arab States as Mideast Conflict Widens
item.description:
Iranian officials will meet on Monday in Oman with representatives of some of the Gulf Arab states that it has repeatedly attacked during its war with the United States and Israel, as the regional conflict has widened in recent days.

Yemen has emerged as the latest front in the fighting, with the Iranian-backed Houthi militants there seizing the strategic port of Mokha and the island of Perim in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea last week. They have also attacked Saudi energy sites and sought to blockade Saudi shipping, exacerbating a global oil and gas crisis prompted by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

Saudi Arabia was forced to shut its East-West Pipeline on Friday after it was targeted by drones from Iraq. That pipeline has been a critical lifeline for the country’s oil exports after Iran effectively blockaded the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf. No one took responsibility for the drone attack, but Iraq has long harbored well-armed militias backed by Iran.

The meeting in Oman will take place as talks with the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have stalled. Iran has continued to fire on ships passing through the strait, squeezing the Gulf Arab states and roiling global oil markets. Last week, the price of Brent crude, the international benchmark, briefly exceeded $110 a barrel, its highest level for months, before dropping to about $104 on Sunday.

Esmaeil Baghaei, the Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman, said last week that the meeting would be held in Oman, which has often served as a mediator between the United States and Iran. Participating countries would discuss efforts by Iran and Oman to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, he added.

Even if an agreement is reached, however, Iranian officials have demanded concessions from the United States before ending their blockade, including lifting sanctions on Iran and releasing frozen U.S. assets. The Trump administration is unlikely to take those steps without Iranian moving to curb its nuclear program.

It was unclear which Arab states would attend the meeting. Mr. Baghaei said officials from Iraq and other Arab states along the Persian Gulf would be involved.

Iran has repeatedly attacked some of those countries since the war began, saying it was targeting the U.S. soldiers and military assets they hosted.

Bahrain, which has repeatedly been targeted by Iranian missiles and drones during the war, said in a statement on Saturday that it would not participate in any talks with Iran.

“The kingdom has been subjected to attacks targeting its infrastructure and civilian assets,” the Bahraini Foreign Ministry said in a statement, adding that any such dialogue would have to be based on “disregarding facts.”

Other countries that have been targeted, however, have signaled that they are open to dialogue. Crown Prince Khaled bin Mohamed Al Nahyan, the Emirati heir apparent, met with President Masoud Pezeshkian of Iran on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in India on Saturday — the first public meeting between the countries since the beginning of the war.

Ship operators still face severe risks in the region. On Sunday, a vessel was struck by a projectile while traveling through the Strait of Hormuz, causing a fire to break out, according to United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, a monitoring group run by the British Navy. It was unclear who had fired on the ship.

item.title: How Iran’s Hard-Liners Prevailed and Sabotaged U.S. Peace Deal
item.description:
Masoud Pezeshkian, the president of Iran, was riding high in early July, fresh off the successful negotiation of a peace agreement with the United States, and had traveled to neighboring Iraq for part of a weeklong funeral spectacle for Iran’s slain supreme leader.

Suddenly he got stunning news.

Iranian forces had opened fire on three commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, setting ablaze a Qatari L.N.G. tanker and damaging other vessels. Iran was under siege in world opinion.

Outraged, Mr. Pezeshkian phoned Gen. Ahmad Vahidi, the commander in chief of the powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, and in a raised voice called the actions reckless and demanded answers, according to five Iranian officials and two Guards members familiar with the events.

General Vahidi told the president that he had neither authorized nor had advance knowledge of the strike, the five officials said. The nation’s Supreme National Security Council, which plays a critical role in both the war and negotiations, had also been in the dark, he said.

In fact, much of the country’s leadership was unaware that a fringe hard-line faction had decided to act on its own. Ultimately, those clandestine efforts derailed a push by more moderate pragmatists in Iran to reach an end to hostilities with the United States and repair their nation’s ailing economy.

The hard-liners succeeded in part because the only figure with the authority to resolve such disputes — the new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei — has been a phantom since taking office in March. He has not been seen, and his voice has not been heard. And the authenticity of written statements and messages attributed to Ayatollah Khamenei has been questioned, including by Mr. Pezeshkian, according to three Iranian officials.

Mr. Pezeshkian immediately returned to Tehran. By the next morning, even as the funeral ceremonies were still underway, the United States had retaliated with airstrikes on Iran. The two countries were back at war.

Senior Iranian officials and a Guards member said in interviews that what followed were some of the most volatile political confrontations within Iran’s leadership in memory. Officials engaged in shouting matches. Two senior generals threatened to resign. Accusations of treason and betrayal flew.

The reverberations, officials said, contributed to a shake-up at the National Security Council and the supreme leader’s appointment of Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, a seasoned politician and former commander in chief of the Guards, to lead the council, as he was thought to have the skill to mediate among political factions.

But divisions persist, and the hard-liners who have committed Iran to escalation are in an even stronger position. This past week, Iran and the United States traded attacks, with Iran repeatedly targeting American naval vessels for the first time, and the United States blowing up at least eight Iranian oil tankers.

This account of the inner deliberations of Iran’s leadership is based on interviews with eight Iranian officials, three members of the Revolutionary Guards, four former officials and a review of dozens of speeches and comments by government officials and military generals from June to September published in the Iranian press and social media. The officials interviewed for this article spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss delicate issues of national security.

Three Iranian officials said inquiries by the government and security forces traced the decision to strike the three commercial ships in July to the cleric Hossein Taeb, an influential spymaster who had opposed the peace deal with the United States from the outset. Mr. Taeb had been telling the new supreme leader that Iran had made a mistake in ending the war and agreeing to the deal, they said.

Mr. Taeb, in a recent speech to military families, said that he was not opposed to talks but that “negotiations that ignore the rights of our people and concede to the excessive demands of the enemy have no place in Iran’s politics.”

Ayatollah Khamenei recently appointed Mr. Taeb as the head of the Basij militia, which is responsible for quelling domestic dissent. He had previously served for more than 20 years as chief for the Revolutionary Guards’ intelligence agency before the previous supreme leader ousted him in 2022 over failures such as Israeli infiltration of his rank and file, and a foiled plot in Turkey. Mr. Taeb re-emerged after that supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed at the start of the war, and he played a key role in the selection of the son Mojtaba as the successor to his father, officials said at the time.

“The attack on the ships was orchestrated with the goal to blow up the memorandum of understanding with Trump and to kill the prospects of any future negotiations and deal,” Alireza Namvar Haghighi, an Iran expert and former official who still has close contacts in the government, said in an interview from Canada.

When Mr. Pezeshkian demanded to know who had struck the three ships, he was told that commanders in the field had acted on their own, in line with an order empowering them to attack any ship violating Iran’s control of the Strait without waiting for approval from central command, according to the officials with knowledge of these discussions. In one sign of the dispute, the Guards’ Khatam al-Anbiya headquarters never issued a statement claiming responsibility for the July 7 attack, as has been routine in other attacks before and since.

Iranian officials relayed this same account to the United States and some of its regional allies in the immediate hours after the attacks, blaming rogue operators, according to U.S. officials who briefed reporters at the time and the three Iranian officials. Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, was dispatched to Oman, a key mediator, to try to defuse tensions with Washington.

On the streets and on state television in Iran, meanwhile, the hard-liners openly attacked the negotiating team and its peace deal, and at nightly rallies, crowds chanted for a return to war.

The Iranian government has devised an official narrative deflecting blame for the collapse of the agreement, saying Washington violated it first by not stopping Israel’s attacks on the militant group Hezbollah in Lebanon, by withholding Iran’s frozen assets and by sneaking ships through a portion of the Strait of Hormuz not controlled by Iran. But few inside Iran’s political circles are convinced by this version, including Mr. Pezeshkian himself, five officials said.

Mr. Pezeshkian said publicly last month that every agreement sees violations and that they should be addressed through talks, not confrontation. When he was privately told by generals that Ayatollah Khamenei had approved the July attack on the three ships, the president demanded proof, according to three Iranian officials.

Under the Iranian form of government, the supreme leader has ultimate authority to settle internal disputes. But Ayatollah Khamenei’s whereabouts, his physical health and mental acuity, and the extent he is involved in state affairs have become subjects of fevered speculation.

“The security situation requires for him to be protected, but I’m asking, how long is this supposed to go on? Six months? One year? Five years? Ten years?” Hojatoleslam Alireza Pirouzmand, a senior cleric and academic at Iran’s National Defense University, said on state television in late July. He added that if “we can’t see our leader, then we will remain in a perpetual state of weakness and decline.”

This month Ayatollah Khamenei’s mother-in-law, Tayebeh Mahrouzadeh, gave a lengthy video interview to a local reporter, describing the extreme security precautions surrounding family members and saying they had no news of the ayatollah and his three children. Her husband, the politician Gholam-Ali Haddad Adel, told the Iranian news media in July that while Ayatollah Khamenei had no contact with anyone for security reasons, “God willing, he is healthy.”

The few comments attributed to the missing leader about the peace deal have added fuel to the dispute. After the agreement was signed, a statement in his name was issued saying he had approved because it had been endorsed by the president and a majority of the National Security Council — but that he was of a different opinion “on principle.” That phrase — “on principle” — has been repeatedly used by hard-liners to attack the deal.

In May, Mr. Pezeshkian said he met with Ayatollah Khamenei but did not say when or where. Two Iranian officials and a former official said the circumstances of the encounter were bizarre.

They said an ambulance with blacked-out windows was used to drive Mr. Pezeshkian around, while a secure video connection was established. A person who said he was an interlocutor for Ayatollah Khamenei appeared on a monitor and purportedly passed messages between the two men.

Mr. Pezeshkian confided to a close ally that he was unsure whether he had actually been communicating with the supreme leader, according to the officials with knowledge of the meeting.

Last month Mr. Pezeshkian said he had been granted a second meeting and that it had lasted for seven hours. “We spoke about all the issues facing the country,” the president told Iran’s state television, listing them as affordability, unemployment, sanctions, unity and resilience during wartime. He did not describe the circumstances of the meeting or reveal what Ayatollah Khamenei had said.

For weeks, the political leaders and generals running Iran have debated two ways to break the stalemate with the United States, officials said.

Under one approach, Iran could seek to return to negotiations. Under the other, it would escalate attacks on American targets, aiming to strike naval vessels, kill American troops and raise global oil prices.

Both would aim to end the U.S. naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports, which have paralyzed trade and brought oil sales down to zero, according to officials. Iran’s economy is deteriorating, with the currency plunging daily, inflation soaring and the government facing a cash deficit.

Hard-line generals, including Brig. Gen. Seyyed Majid Mousavi, who commands the Guards’ Aerospace Force, pressed for confrontation, officials and two Guards members said. The generals told the National Security Council they had devised a detailed war plan in which Iran and allied militias, in particular the Houthis in Yemen and armed Shiite Muslim groups in Iraqi, would intensify attacks, including on regional oil facilities, further widening the scope of the war and raising its costs for the United States and its allies.

Mr. Pezeshkian and Gen. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who is the speaker of Parliament and the top negotiator with the United States, were among the officials who warned that the war plan risked dragging the country into an abyss, with even fiercer U.S. airstrikes and more crippling economic pressure.

But by last Saturday, the hard-line faction had gained the upper hand. “The war between Iran and the United States,” said Mahdi Mohammadi, the top adviser to General Ghalibaf, “has entered the phase of escalation.”
